tip: In ci vediamo, ci means each other: we see each other. Ci can also mean us, there, or about it depending on context.
The noi form doubles as English 'let's': parliamo means both 'we talk' and 'let's talk'.
Facevo sport covers more than 'was exercising': the imperfetto also carries 'used to exercise' and habitual 'would exercise'.
Hanno pulito looks like 'have cleaned', but spoken Italian uses the passato prossimo as the plain everyday past: 'they cleaned'.
A past-tense opener like Pensavo che pushes the subjunctive into its past form: fosse, not sia.
Wishes take vorrei che plus the past subjunctive: Vorrei che fosse means 'I wish it were'.
Reflexives build the past with essere, and the participle matches the speaker: Mi sono svegliato (m), svegliata (f).
Repeated past events take the imperfetto: arrivava sempre = 'always arrived', not the one-off passato prossimo.
Sembra che (it seems that) flips the following verb to the subjunctive: capiscano, not capiscono.
Verbs of motion take essere, and the participle shows who moved: È corsa means a woman ran, corso for a man.
Negative tu commands use non plus the infinitive: Non aprire, not the normal command form apri.
The imperfetto describes an ongoing background: Passavamo le sere means 'we used to spend the evenings', a habit rather than a single event.
Riposarsi is reflexive: literally 'rest oneself', so Ti riposi keeps the ti where English just says 'you rest'.
Sempre signals a past habit, so the verb goes imperfetto: portava sempre means 'she always wore'.
When two pronouns stack, indirect comes before direct: ve lo means 'it to you', both sitting before ripeto.
English 'I preferred' is simple past, but an ongoing preference needs the imperfetto in Italian: preferivo.
Present tense plus da expresses duration: Abita da tre anni means 'he has been living for three years', still ongoing.
Bisogna che (it's necessary that) forces the subjunctive: io faccia, not faccio.
Sembra che (it seems that) triggers the subjunctive on the next verb: cambi, not cambia.
Bisogna che states a real need, but the action stays hypothetical, so it takes the subjunctive: migliori, not migliora.
With an infinitive, the reflexive si attaches to the end: lavarsi means 'to wash oneself'.
Italian usually drops subject pronouns; Lui and io appear only for contrast: Lui studiava means HE studied, while I slept.
Prendine is prendi plus ne, where ne stands for 'of them': prendine means 'take one of them'.
Credo che (I believe that) triggers the subjunctive: faccia bel tempo, not fa.
English drops the pronoun in 'the house I live in', but Italian must keep it: la casa in cui vivo.
Mi already means 'to me', so no preposition is needed: Mi ha detto is 'he told to me'.
'Even though' words like nonostante force the subjunctive: faccia caldo, not fa caldo.
Vorremmo is the conditional of volere, 'we would like': softer and more polite than the blunt vogliamo, 'we want'.
Nonostante forces the subjunctive even for a plain fact: sia stanco means 'I'm tired', though English changes nothing.
Impersonal judgments like è meglio che demand the subjunctive: tu faccia, where English just says 'you do'.
Da' questo libro uses the short tu command: da', di', fa', va', sta' all cut to one syllable, the apostrophe marking the drop.
Parliamo means both 'we talk' and 'let's talk'; same form, and context picks the suggestion reading here.
The non in a meno che non cambi is not a negation; it belongs to 'unless', so this means 'unless I change my mind', not 'unless I don't'.
Dovreste is conditional dovere, 'you should': soft advice, versus dovete, 'you must'.
English drops 'that' in 'the train I take', but che is mandatory in Italian: il treno che prendo.
Singular family members drop the article with a possessive: tua sorella, not la tua sorella; plurals keep it.
After a preposition you can't use che; it becomes preposition plus article plus quale: con il quale.
Conditional potere is the polite 'could': potrebbe aiutarmi means 'could you help me', the go-to softener with strangers.
Farsi means to do something for yourself: mi farei un bagno is 'I'd run myself a bath', a reflexive where English has none.
To forbid, Italian switches to the infinitive: parla means 'speak', but Non parlare means 'don't speak'.
The negative tu command uses the infinitive with the pronoun glued on: Non dirgli means 'don't tell him'.
Mi piacerebbe is literally 'it would please me': the thing liked is the subject, and the wanter is mi.
After quando Italian keeps the future: Quando avrò tempo is literally 'when I will have time', where English uses the present.
The future perfect of a motion verb uses essere: sarò partito means 'I'll have left', never avrò.
Spoken Italian often uses the present for the future: instead of cucinerò you could just say 'stasera cucino'.
Quello che means 'what', the thing that: quello che mi serviva is 'what I needed', with no specific noun behind it.
